newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU plans to clear Finnish timber deal.
newsitem.headline: EU plans to clear Finnish timber deal.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it planned to approve for five years an amended deal on long-term development of competition in the roundwood trade in Finland.
The agreement was notified by the Finnish Forest Industries' Federation and the Central Union of Agricultural Producers and Forest Owners (MTK).
Before clearing it, however, the EU executive said in its Official Journal it invited third parties to comment.
The Commission could authorise the deal only after it was amended by the MTK and the Federation last June.
This came after the Commission had sent a so called warning letter informing them that their planned regional agreements could restrict competition.

Under the amended plan, these regional agreements will be abandoned and replaced by deals negotiated between forestry firms and representatives of the forest owners from the companies' operating areas.
"The purpose of these negotiations is to reach a common understanding of the market situation and of price expectations," the Commission said.

"In contrast with the previous arrangements, forest industry undertakings do not cooperate in any pricing issues or participate as a group in the negotiations, or in any capacity connected to the negotiations," it said.
The Finnish roundwood market is characterised by a large imbalance in the negotiating power of sellers and buyers.
On the sellers' side there are hundreds of thousands of small forest owners while the buyers' side is normally represented by a few large forest firms.

"Given this special situation in the Finnish forest sector and in order to to meet the objective of creating and maintaining confidence amongst forest owners, so that the raw material supply is secured, a mechanism has been worked out whereby some form of cooperation is allowed," it said.
The MTK and the Federation first notified agreements on the development of trade in wood and also one-year agreements on price rises and felling volumes in March 1994.

However, the Surveillance Autority of the European Free Trade Association -- to which Finland belonged at the time -- considered that it was a question of a price cartel and market-sharing arrangement.
The issue came under the competence of the Commission after Finland joined the EU in January 1995.
